support.corpus: Umbrian (via Buck's grammar; not found in the ikuvina UD file)

words.lemma: formnae 'pick, choicest part' (nom. pl.; unmapped in slab)
slaidid 'strikes, slays', s-pret. 1sg. with infixed pron.

words.etymon: renewal of *wiHró- (cf. a-vīra-hā in the same verse)

cognate: All three nouns of the Irish list are exact cognates of the Indic list: Ir. bó ~ Skt. gáv-/go- (*gʷṓws), Ir. fer ~ Skt. vīrá- (*wiHrós), Ir. ech ~ Skt. áśva- (*h₁éḱwos).
drift_or_renewal: In AVŚ 1.16.4 (slab s9) the 'man' slot is filled by pūruṣa-, a renewal, but vīra- comes back in the same verse in a-vīra-hā 'slayer of (our) men'; AVŚ 12.2.29 and RV 1.114.8 keep vīrá-. The verb is renewed on the Irish side: slaidid (and do-tuit 'fall' in darochratar) where Indic has han- (*gʷʰen-) and vadh-. Homer (Il. 9.406-8) has ἀνήρ for the 'man' slot.
shared_syntax: A coordinated list of three nouns (cattle, man, horse) for the living wealth of a community, given as the victims of a killing verb: in Irish the list is the subject of do-rochratar 'fell (by my hands)' and is taken up by the object pronoun of roda slaidius 'I slew them'; in AVŚ 1.16.4 it is the object of haṃsi 'you kill'; in AVŚ 12.2.29 and RV 1.114.8 it sits in the locative ('in our cows, in our horses, in our men') with a verb of harm (rīriṣaḥ / vadhīḥ).
context: Cú Chulainn's lament over Fer Diad (Táin Bó Cúailnge, Book of Leinster version, poem 'Cluiche cách, gáine cách', lines 29-32): 'trí díríme na Tána / darochratar dom láma, / formna bó fer ⁊ ech, / roda slaidius ar cech leth': the countless hosts of the Táin fell by his hands, the pick of cattle, men and horses. The AV verses are protective charms against a demon or a corpse-eating fire that kills a community's cows, horses and men. RV 1.114.8 is the same plea to Rudra. The match is not just 'what a raid kills': all three slots are filled by the canonical cognate set, in the same order of species, and the list stands under a verb of slaying on both sides. The two-term core, men + cattle, is the recognised IE merism (Umbr. ueiro pequo; Av. pasu- vīra-), and Irish and Indic both extend it with the horse. Caveats: the Irish is a Middle Irish LL poem (12th-c. manuscript) and the AV verses are charms, so the congruence is 'living wealth destroyed', not one identical speech act. The list is semantically natural for pastoral societies, which limits how much it proves.
phrase: Ir. formna bó fer ⁊ ech … roda slaidius ~ AVŚ yadi no gāṃ haṃsi yady aśvaṃ yadi pūruṣam / yo no aśveṣu vīreṣu yo no goṣu ~ RV mā́ no góṣu mā́ no áśveṣu rīriṣaḥ, vīrā́n mā́ no … vadhīḥ: 'cattle, men and horses' as victims of slaying

note: All 174 bundles (every pivot Middle Irish) read in order. One claim: BC-e807e, the cattle-men-horses triad (Ir. bó fer ⁊ ech ~ AV/RV gáv- vīrá- áśva-) under a verb of slaying, medium. Rejected as generic or late: BC-7b296 snow/coal simile (ON witness is Barlaam, translated prose); BC-7031b cows milked for a guest (βοῦς ἀμέλγεσθαι); BC-c544b worm in the head ~ AV worm charm (bare death notice); TBC sky-falls oath (BC-1a629, BC-b2950) has no non-Celtic partner in the slab.
